title: The inverse-square precision scaling law for sample size
scenario_markdown: A hospital administration team surveys outpatient waiting times. In the initial survey round, a sample size of $n = 100$ yielded a margin of error of $E = 10\text{ minutes}$ at the $95\%$ confidence level. Hospital leadership announces a continuous improvement initiative and requests that the subsequent survey achieve twice the precision, cutting the margin of error in half to $E_{\text{new}} = 5\text{ minutes}$, while maintaining the same $95\%$ confidence level and assuming the population variance $\sigma^2$ remains unchanged.

parameters.objective: Understand why halving margin of error requires quadrupling sample size

assumptions: Population standard deviation sigma and confidence level remain unchanged between surveys

approval.notes: Reviewed conceptual relationship between margin of error and sample size. Because n = (z*sigma/E)^2, replacing E with E/2 multiplies n by (1/(1/2))^2 = 4. Highlights diminishing marginal returns in data collection.

stages.prompt_markdown: By what factor must the hospital multiply its initial sample size ($n = 100$) to reduce the margin of error by half (from $10\text{ minutes}$ to $5\text{ minutes}$)?

options.hint_markdown: Sample size depends inversely on the square of the margin of error ($n \propto 1/E^2$), not linearly on $1/E$.
While standard error scales with $1/\sqrt{n}$, solving for $n$ squares the reciprocal of the margin of error factor: $(2)^2 = 4$.
The power on the margin of error in the sample size formula is quadratic ($E^2$), not cubic.

stages.explanation_markdown: The sample size formula is $n = \left(\frac{z\sigma}{E}\right)^2$. If the margin of error is halved to $E' = E/2$, then $n' = \left(\frac{z\sigma}{E/2}\right)^2 = 4 \left(\frac{z\sigma}{E}\right)^2 = 4n$. Halving the margin of error requires quadrupling the sample size from $100$ to $400$.

stages.prompt_markdown: What fundamental principle of inferential statistics explains why doubling survey precision requires four times as much data?

options.text_markdown: Because the standard error of the sample mean decreases only with the square root of sample size ($SE = \sigma / \sqrt{n}$), creating diminishing returns to sample size.
Because degrees of freedom grow slower than the sample size itself.
options.hint_markdown: Degrees of freedom grow linearly ($n-1$), which actually stabilizes critical values rather than creating the quadratic sample requirement.

options.text_markdown: Because sampling without replacement alters the population variance as the sample grows.
options.hint_markdown: The quadratic scaling law holds even in infinite or very large populations where FPC does not apply.

options.text_markdown: Because the significance level $\alpha$ must be cut in half whenever the margin of error is halved.
options.hint_markdown: The confidence level (and $\alpha$) remains unchanged at $95\%$; the margin of error relates to sample size, not $\alpha$.

stages.explanation_markdown: The Central Limit Theorem dictates that the variability of sample averages shrinks at the rate of $1/\sqrt{n}$. To cut the spread in half, $\sqrt{n}$ must double, which requires $n$ to quadruple. This mathematical property produces diminishing marginal returns to data collection in all empirical research.
